questions.stem: A 38 year old man had a painful, swollen left calf for 4 days after a flight from Australia. Today he has sudden sharp left-sided chest pain on breathing in and has coughed up a small amount of blood. His pulse rate is 112 bpm, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. His chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A swollen, painful calf followed by pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, tachycardia and hypoxia is the classic pattern of PE.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: coughed up a small amount of blood
steps.x: Leg DVT then chest symptoms, with a clear chest.

elim: Would cause fever, purulent sputum and focal crackles; his chest is clear.
Haemoptysis at 38 with a sudden onset after a flight points to embolism.
Pain eases on sitting forward; no calf swelling or hypoxia link.
Would give reduced breath sounds and hyperresonance.

steps.x: **D. Pulmonary embolism.** Calf swelling then pleuritic pain and haemoptysis = PE.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has a large pulmonary embolism confirmed on CTPA 10 days after a hip replacement. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 104/68 mmHg and oxygen saturation 90% on 4 L/min oxygen. Her jugular venous pressure is raised 6 cm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
o: Loud P2 with a left parasternal heave
Stony dullness at the right base
questions.e: A large PE causes right heart strain: raised JVP, a left parasternal heave and a loud pulmonary second sound.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Large clot load with a raised JVP: the right ventricle is struggling.

elim: Suggest pulmonary oedema from left heart failure.
Suggests pericarditis.
Suggest pneumothorax.
Suggests a large pleural effusion.

steps.x: **B. Loud P2 with a left parasternal heave.** Right heart strain in PE: raised JVP, parasternal heave, loud P2.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has sudden breathlessness 2 weeks after a knee arthroscopy. His pulse rate is 122 bpm and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. CTPA shows large bilateral pulmonary emboli with a dilated right ventricle.
questions.q: Which ECG pattern of right heart strain is most likely?
o: Deep S in I, Q wave and inverted T in III
Delta waves with a short PR interval
Saddle-shaped ST elevation in all leads
ST depression in V5 and V6 with tall R waves
questions.e: The classic (though less common) ECG of PE is S1Q3T3, reflecting acute right ventricular strain; sinus tachycardia is the commonest finding.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
A big clot load straining the right ventricle.

elim: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.
Seen with a large pericardial effusion.
Pericarditis.
Left ventricular hypertrophy with strain.

steps.x: **A. Deep S in I, Q wave and inverted T in III.** PE ECG: sinus tachycardia most often; classic S1Q3T3 with RV strain.

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman has 2 days of breathlessness and fainting on climbing stairs. She is recovering from an ovarian cancer operation 2 weeks ago. Her pulse rate is 116 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. Her chest is clear and her troponin is mildly raised. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Sinus tachycardia with T wave inversion in V1 to V3: right ventricular strain.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sinus tachycardia with T wave inversion in V1 to V3 reflects right ventricular strain in PE, here provoked by cancer surgery.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Post-op cancer patient, hypoxic with a clear chest, ECG showing right-sided strain.

elim: Would show ST elevation in V1 to V4, not isolated T wave inversion with this history.
A chronic condition; the timing after cancer surgery points to embolism.
Widespread saddle ST elevation and pleuritic pain eased by sitting forward.
Would cause absent breath sounds on one side.

steps.x: **D. Pulmonary embolism.** T wave inversion V1–V3 + tachycardia + hypoxia = PE with RV strain.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman is 5 days after an abdominal hysterectomy. She has sudden pain in the right side of her chest on breathing in. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. Her chest is clear and her chest X-ray is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pleuritic pain, tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypoxia and a low-grade fever with a normal X-ray after surgery is PE.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Post-op, hypoxic, low-grade fever, but the lungs look normal.

elim: Common early after surgery but does not cause marked hypoxia with sudden pleuritic pain.
Does not cause tachycardia, tachypnoea or hypoxia.
Would usually show consolidation, crackles and a higher fever.
Would show on the chest X-ray.

steps.x: **D. Pulmonary embolism.** Hypoxia + clear chest + normal CXR after surgery = think PE.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has a pulmonary embolism confirmed on CTPA. Over the next 20 minutes, despite 2 L of fluid, his BP stays at 82/50 mmHg. His pulse rate is 132 bpm and oxygen saturation 86% on 15 L/min oxygen. Echocardiography shows a dilated right ventricle.
questions.q: Which feature defines this as a massive pulmonary embolism?
o: Systolic BP below 90 mmHg for over 15 minutes
questions.e: Massive PE is defined by persistent hypotension (systolic below 90 mmHg for more than 15 minutes) or collapse.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Sustained hypotension despite fluid.

elim: Shows RV strain but also occurs in submassive PE.
Common in all PEs.
Common in all PEs and not defining.
Marks RV strain but does not define massive PE.

steps.x: **E. Systolic BP below 90 mmHg for over 15 minutes.** Massive PE = systolic <90 mmHg for >15 min or collapse.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman has a pulmonary embolism confirmed on CTPA. She has not travelled, had surgery or taken hormones. She has lost 7 kg in 3 months and has had postmenopausal bleeding. Her haemoglobin and platelet count are normal and she has no proteinuria.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Cancer is a major risk factor for PE; weight loss and postmenopausal bleeding suggest endometrial cancer.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
PE with red flags for cancer.

elim: A first unprovoked clot at 71 with weight loss and bleeding points to cancer.
She has not had heparin and platelets are normal.
No proteinuria.
Her haemoglobin is normal.

steps.x: **E. Underlying malignancy.** PE risk factors include cancer; look for it if red flags.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman who takes the combined oral contraceptive pill has sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. Her pulse rate is 114 bpm and respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute. Arterial blood gas breathing air is shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of the blood gas?
questions.e: PE causes hypoxaemia and hyperventilation, giving a low PaO2, low PaCO2 and a raised pH: respiratory alkalosis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Hyperventilating and hypoxic with a likely PE.

elim: pH is high, not low, and bicarbonate is normal.
Bicarbonate is normal; the change is respiratory.
PaO2 and PaCO2 are both low.
PaCO2 is low, not high.

steps.x: **E. Respiratory alkalosis with hypoxaemia.** PE ABG: low PaO2, low PaCO2, respiratory alkalosis.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman collapses while walking to the bus stop and recovers in under a minute. She started the combined oral contraceptive pill 2 months ago. She now feels breathless. Her pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 102/64 mmHg and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia and her blood glucose is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her collapse?
questions.e: PE can present with syncope; persistent tachycardia and hypoxia in a woman on the COCP point to it.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Syncope followed by breathlessness, tachycardia and hypoxia.

elim: Her blood glucose is normal.
Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia only, and that would not cause persistent hypoxia.
No tonic-clonic movements, and hypoxia persists after recovery.
Would recover fully, without ongoing tachycardia and hypoxia.

steps.x: **C. Pulmonary embolism.** Syncope + persistent hypoxia + oestrogen = PE.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man with a confirmed pulmonary embolism becomes drowsy. His BP is 76/44 mmHg, pulse rate 136 bpm and JVP raised to his earlobes. His lungs are clear. Bedside echocardiography shows a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle with tricuspid regurgitation and a small, underfilled left ventricle.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his hypotension?
o: Cardiogenic shock from left ventricular infarction
Obstructive shock from right heart failure
questions.e: Massive PE blocks pulmonary outflow; the right ventricle fails and the left ventricle underfills, causing obstructive shock.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
High JVP, clear lungs and a struggling right heart.

elim: No rash, wheeze or allergen exposure.
Echo would show pericardial fluid.
The left ventricle is small and underfilled, not failing.
His JVP is very high, not low.

steps.x: **E. Obstructive shock from right heart failure.** Massive PE: RV failure and obstructive shock.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has sudden pleuritic left chest pain and breathlessness after a 12-hour flight. His pulse rate is 108 bpm and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. A CTPA is booked for later that morning. A chest X-ray is done first.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
o: Clear lung fields with no abnormality
questions.e: In PE the chest X-ray is usually normal; its role is to exclude other causes.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Likely PE after a long flight.

elim: Seen in sarcoidosis or lymphoma.
A small effusion can occur in PE, but a large one is not typical.
Points to pneumonia.
Would be a different diagnosis.

steps.x: **B. Clear lung fields with no abnormality.** PE: CXR usually normal (used to exclude other pathology).

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman on a stroke rehabilitation ward has been unable to walk for 9 days. She suddenly becomes breathless and anxious. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air. Her chest is clear and her right calf is swollen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Immobility after stroke is a provoking factor; sudden breathlessness with hypoxia, a clear chest and a swollen calf is PE.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Immobile, hypoxic, clear chest, DVT signs.

elim: Would give bibasal crackles.
Does not cause hypoxia.
Would give fever, crackles and often a history of choking.
Would give wheeze.

steps.x: **D. Pulmonary embolism.** Immobility + sudden hypoxia + clear chest = PE.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man is having chemotherapy for pancreatic cancer. For 3 days he has been more breathless walking around the house. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. His chest is clear, the chest X-ray is normal and his haemoglobin is 128 g/L (130–180).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his breathlessness?
questions.e: Active cancer is a strong provoking factor; unexplained tachycardia and hypoxia with a normal X-ray suggests PE.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Cancer patient, hypoxic, normal X-ray.

elim: His haemoglobin is only slightly low and would not cause hypoxia.
Usually shows interstitial shadowing on the X-ray.
Would show on the X-ray.
He is afebrile.

steps.x: **D. Pulmonary embolism.** Active cancer + unexplained hypoxia and tachycardia = PE until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman with a BMI of 43 kg/m² has had a cough and sharp right-sided chest pain for 1 day. She has been off work and mostly in bed for 2 weeks with a back injury. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Her chest is clear and her calves are hard to assess.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Obesity and immobilisation are provoking factors; cough, pleuritic pain, tachycardia and hypoxia with a clear chest suggest PE.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Obesity and immobility with pleuritic pain and hypoxia.

elim: Does not cause hypoxia or tachycardia of this degree.
Does not cause hypoxia.
Pain eases sitting forward, without hypoxia.
Would give focal crackles and a higher fever.

steps.x: **D. Pulmonary embolism.** Obesity + immobility = provoked PE risk.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. There is no other likely diagnosis. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. Her calves are normal, with no swelling or tenderness. She has no cancer, haemoptysis or recent surgery and no previous VTE. Her 2-level Wells score is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: 2-level Wells score for PE
visual.label: Score 4.5
visual.caption: Above 4: PE likely, so go straight to CTPA.

questions.q: Which is her 2-level Wells score?
questions.e: PE most likely diagnosis (+3) and heart rate over 100 (+1.5) = 4.5, so PE likely (>4): go straight to CTPA.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Add up: PE most likely 3, HR >100 1.5, no DVT signs.

elim: Only counts the heart rate.
Only counts 'PE most likely'.
Would need clinical DVT signs, which she does not have (they add 3).
Adds DVT signs she does not have.

steps.x: **C. 4.5.** Wells >4 = PE likely: CTPA.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has suspected pulmonary embolism with a 2-level Wells score of 6. He had anaphylaxis to iodinated contrast during a previous CT scan. His eGFR is 88 mL/min/1.73m² and his chest X-ray is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: If CTPA is unsuitable (contrast allergy, renal impairment, pregnancy), a V/Q scan is used.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
PE likely but contrast is unsafe.

elim: He had anaphylaxis to iodinated contrast.
With Wells >4 imaging is needed, and D-dimer cannot confirm PE.
Can show RV strain but cannot exclude or confirm PE.
Do not diagnose PE.

steps.x: **E. Ventilation/perfusion scan.** CTPA unsuitable: V/Q scan.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has 2 days of mild pleuritic chest pain. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. His 2-level Wells score is 3, because PE is thought the most likely diagnosis. A D-dimer is raised.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
questions.e: With Wells ≤4, D-dimer is first; a positive result needs CTPA, because D-dimer is sensitive but not specific.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
PE unlikely but D-dimer is positive.

elim: A positive D-dimer means PE has not been excluded.
Not a diagnostic test for PE.
Will not change management; imaging is needed.
He is stable and PE is unconfirmed.

steps.x: **A. CT pulmonary angiogram.** Wells ≤4 + positive D-dimer = CTPA.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has a 2-level Wells score of 1.5 for suspected pulmonary embolism. She was given a dose of apixaban while waiting for results. Her D-dimer is negative. She now feels better, with a pulse rate of 86 bpm and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
o: Stop anticoagulation and consider another diagnosis
questions.e: Wells ≤4 with a negative D-dimer excludes PE: stop interim anticoagulation and look for another cause.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Low probability and negative D-dimer.

elim: PE has been excluded.
Not needed: low probability and negative D-dimer exclude PE.
Not needed.
Not needed.

steps.x: **D. Stop anticoagulation and consider another diagnosis.** Wells ≤4 + negative D-dimer: PE excluded, stop anticoagulation.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant has sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. Her left calf is swollen and tender. Her pulse rate is 106 bpm, BP 114/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Compression duplex ultrasound of the legs
questions.e: In pregnancy with suspected PE and signs of DVT, compression duplex ultrasound is first-line: a DVT confirms VTE without chest radiation.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.

clues: left calf is swollen and tender
steps.x: Pregnant with DVT signs.

elim: Avoided as the first test when DVT signs allow a leg scan with no radiation.
Normally raised in pregnancy.
Does not diagnose PE.
Used if leg imaging is negative, not first when DVT signs are present.

steps.x: **A. Compression duplex ultrasound of the legs.** Pregnant + PE symptoms + DVT signs: leg ultrasound first.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man has sudden breathlessness 2 weeks after a knee replacement. His 2-level Wells score is 7.5. His pulse rate is 110 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. CTPA cannot be done for 6 hours. He has normal renal function and no bleeding risk.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management while awaiting imaging?
questions.e: With strong clinical suspicion and a delay in imaging, start interim treatment-dose anticoagulation such as rivaroxaban.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
PE likely, stable, imaging delayed.

elim: Not anticoagulation for VTE.
Leaves a likely PE untreated.
He is haemodynamically stable.
Takes days to work and needs heparin cover.

steps.x: **B. Interim rivaroxaban.** Delay in imaging: interim DOAC (e.g. rivaroxaban).

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has pleuritic chest pain and a swollen, tender left calf after a long coach journey. Her 2-level Wells score is 6.5. CTPA shows no pulmonary embolism. She is well, with a pulse rate of 90 bpm and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: If CTPA is negative but DVT is still suspected, do a proximal leg vein ultrasound.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
PE excluded but DVT signs remain.

elim: No indication.
Unnecessary radiation; the leg is the question now.
Does not assess the leg.
CTPA has already excluded PE.

steps.x: **B. Proximal leg vein ultrasound.** CTPA negative + suspected DVT: leg ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man has 2 days of left-sided chest pain after moving furniture. He thinks PE is unlikely but is worried. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. He has no leg swelling, haemoptysis, recent surgery or trauma, or previous VTE, and takes no hormones.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: No further testing for pulmonary embolism
questions.e: If clinical probability is low and all PERC criteria are met (age under 50, HR under 100, SpO2 over 94%, no leg swelling, haemoptysis, recent surgery or trauma, previous VTE or oestrogen), PE is excluded.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Young, normal heart rate and saturation, no risk factors: all PERC criteria met.

elim: Not needed when PERC criteria are all met in low-risk patients.
A PERC-negative low-risk patient does not need a D-dimer.
No PE is suspected.
Not needed.

steps.x: **C. No further testing for pulmonary embolism.** PERC negative in a low-risk patient: no further PE tests.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has a small pulmonary embolism confirmed on CTPA after a long-haul flight. He has no cancer, heart failure or chronic lung disease. His pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. The team want to know if he can go home.
questions.q: Which tool should be used to decide if he can be treated as an outpatient?
questions.e: The PESI score (recommended by the BTS) identifies low-risk PE (class 1–2) suitable for outpatient rivaroxaban.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Diagnosis made; now judge severity.

elim: Assesses pneumonia severity.
Used to exclude PE before testing, not after diagnosis.
Estimates the probability of PE before testing.
Estimates DVT probability.

steps.x: **C. PESI score.** PESI: low risk (I–II) can go home on rivaroxaban.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has a pulmonary embolism confirmed on CTPA after a knee replacement. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP 138/84 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Her eGFR is 82 mL/min/1.73m², platelets are normal and she has no bleeding history.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: A DOAC such as apixaban or rivaroxaban is first-line for stable PE with normal renal function and no increased bleeding risk.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Stable, normal kidneys, no bleeding risk.

elim: Thrombolysis is only for massive (haemodynamically unstable) PE.
Not a treatment for PE.
Third line, mainly in severe renal failure.
Needs LMWH bridging; a DOAC is first line.

steps.x: **B. Apixaban.** Stable PE: DOAC first line.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has a pulmonary embolism. She has had two previous miscarriages, and lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies are positive on two occasions 12 weeks apart. She is started on LMWH.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term anticoagulation?
questions.e: PE with antiphospholipid syndrome needs lifelong warfarin, started with LMWH for at least 5 days and until INR 2–3.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.

clues: positive on two occasions 12 weeks apart
steps.x: This is antiphospholipid syndrome.

elim: Too short, and DOACs are not preferred in antiphospholipid syndrome.
Inadequate after a venous thrombosis.
DOACs are not preferred and 6 months is too short.
Antiphospholipid syndrome needs lifelong anticoagulation.

steps.x: **C. Lifelong warfarin.** APS + VTE: lifelong warfarin (LMWH bridge first).

questions.stem: A 59 year old man takes warfarin for previous pulmonary emboli with a target INR of 2.5. He now has a new pulmonary embolism confirmed on CTPA. His INR has been 2.3–2.8 for the last 6 months and he takes his warfarin reliably.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate change to his anticoagulation?
o: Insert an IVC filter and stop warfarin
questions.e: Recurrent VTE on warfarin with a therapeutic INR: increase the target INR to 3–4.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Recurrence despite a therapeutic INR.

elim: Raises bleeding risk without enough benefit.
Filters are for when anticoagulation cannot be given.
He has recurrent VTE.
Inadequate.

steps.x: **C. Raise the target INR to 3–4.** Recurrent VTE on warfarin: target INR 3–4.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has a pulmonary embolism 3 weeks after a laparoscopic appendicectomy. She has no other risk factors and no bleeding risk. She has started apixaban and is stable.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate duration of anticoagulation?
questions.e: A provoked PE is treated for at least 3 months.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Clear, temporary trigger: provoked.

elim: Longer than needed for a clot provoked by a transient factor.
Too short.
For active cancer-associated PE or some unprovoked cases.
For antiphospholipid syndrome or recurrent unprovoked VTE.

steps.x: **B. 3 months.** Provoked PE: at least 3 months.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman who is 24 weeks pregnant has a pulmonary embolism confirmed on V/Q scan. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Her renal function is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: When a DOAC is unsuitable, as in pregnancy, LMWH is used.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Stable PE in pregnancy.

elim: She is stable.
DOACs are not used in pregnancy.
DOACs are not used in pregnancy.
Teratogenic.

steps.x: **C. Low molecular weight heparin.** PE in pregnancy: LMWH.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man is brought to the emergency department with sudden breathlessness and chest pain 10 days after a hip fracture repair. His pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 108/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 84% breathing air. He is alert.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: High-flow oxygen via a non-rebreathe mask
questions.e: Manage with ABCDE first; a hypoxic patient needs 15 L/min oxygen via a non-rebreathe mask.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Very hypoxic but not shocked.

elim: Needed, but only after initial stabilisation.
He is not hypotensive and PE is unconfirmed.
Treatment comes after the ABCDE assessment and oxygen.
Not the priority.

steps.x: **B. High-flow oxygen via a non-rebreathe mask.** PE emergency: ABCDE, high-flow oxygen if hypoxic.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has a massive pulmonary embolism. Her BP is 78/46 mmHg and has been for 25 minutes. She had a haemorrhagic stroke 2 years ago. A cardiothoracic and interventional radiology team are available on site.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Massive PE needs urgent thrombolysis, but a previous haemorrhagic stroke contraindicates it; then consider specialist embolectomy or catheter intervention.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Massive PE with an absolute contraindication to thrombolysis.

elim: Previous haemorrhagic stroke at any time contraindicates thrombolysis.
Too slow for a shocked patient.
Not enough for massive PE.
Also a thrombolytic, so contraindicated.

steps.x: **A. Catheter-directed or surgical embolectomy.** Massive PE, thrombolysis contraindicated: embolectomy or catheter therapy.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man is on unfractionated heparin for a pulmonary embolism. On day 8 his platelet count has fallen from 260 to 90 ×10⁹/L (150–400) and he has a new swollen right arm with a thrombus on ultrasound. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia antibodies are positive.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Stop heparin and start warfarin immediately
questions.e: HIT is a complication of treatment: stop heparin promptly and switch to a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban, with haematology review.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Falling platelets and new thrombosis 5–10 days into heparin.

elim: Heparin drives the reaction and platelets can worsen thrombosis.
HIT is prothrombotic; he needs a non-heparin anticoagulant.
Warfarin alone early can cause venous limb gangrene in HIT.
LMWH cross-reacts with HIT antibodies.

steps.x: **C. Stop heparin and start argatroban.** HIT: stop heparin, start argatroban.

questions.stem: A 53 year old woman with a massive pulmonary embolism is given intravenous alteplase. Her BP was 80/50 mmHg for 20 minutes. She has no contraindications to thrombolysis. The team must choose the anticoagulant to give alongside it.
questions.q: Which anticoagulant is most appropriate?
questions.e: Massive PE is treated with thrombolysis plus IV unfractionated heparin, which acts fast, can be titrated and is reversible.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Unstable patient being thrombolysed.

elim: Oral absorption is unreliable in shock and it cannot be quickly reversed.
Too slow.
Long-acting and not reversible.
Less controllable than IV UFH in an unstable patient.

steps.x: **A. Intravenous unfractionated heparin.** Massive PE: alteplase + IV unfractionated heparin.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man dies suddenly 10 days after a femur fracture. Post-mortem shows a large clot straddling the main pulmonary artery bifurcation. The clot is long and shaped like the vein it formed in.
questions.q: Which is the most likely origin of the clot?
questions.e: Most PEs are DVTs from the leg that embolise via the venous system and right heart to the pulmonary arteries.

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to the underlying mechanism before reading the options.

clues: shaped like the vein it formed in
steps.x: A cast of a vein after a leg fracture.

elim: Left heart clots embolise to the systemic arteries, not the lungs.
Left ventricular thrombus goes to the systemic circulation.
Drain to the left atrium.
Superficial thrombus rarely embolises.

steps.x: **A. Deep veins of the leg.** PE usually starts as a leg DVT.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has a large pulmonary embolism. Echocardiography shows a dilated right ventricle, flattening of the septum and tricuspid regurgitation. A student asks why the right ventricle has dilated.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Left ventricular failure transmitting pressure back
Raised pulmonary vascular resistance increasing RV afterload

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has a pulmonary embolism. Her PaO2 is 8.4 kPa (10–14) and PaCO2 3.5 kPa (4.7–6.0). A student asks why the PaO2 is low even though she is breathing fast and the airways are clear.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her hypoxaemia?
o: Diffusion block from thickened alveolar walls
Reduced oxygen carrying capacity from anaemia
questions.e: The clot blocks perfusion to ventilated alveoli, causing V/Q mismatch; the resulting hypoxaemia drives hyperventilation, so PaCO2 falls (respiratory alkalosis).
